title: The Sewol Ferry Disaster
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck cover the 2014 Sewol ferry disaster off South Korea, released on the twelfth anniversary. The Sewol, a former Japanese ferry, sailed from Incheon to Jeju on April 15, 2014 with 476 people aboard, including 325 Danwon High School students on a class trip (the transcript says 250 eleventh graders). It was overloaded with cargo, its ballast was scuttled, and a sharp turn caused it to list and capsize. The captain and crew ordered passengers to stay in their cabins and the captain abandoned ship early. Only one coast guard boat arrived about 50 minutes after the turn, and fishing boats rescued many survivors before being ordered away. 304 people died. The episode covers the government's response and surveillance of grieving families, the trials and sentences of the captain, crew, ferry company executives and officials, the owner Yoo Byung-eun's flight and death, President Park Geun-hye's conduct and impeachment, the civil settlement, the ship's salvage, the Coast Guard's dissolution, the Memorial classroom, and the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush. The episode ends with a listener mail about homemade deodorant.

segments.title: Introduction to the Sewol disaster
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Sewol ferry disaster as part of a marine disaster series, noting it involved children and was human caused. They describe the scale of the loss and its impact on South Korean society.

segments.title: Danwon High School trip and departure
segments.summary: The students from Danwon High School in Ansan were on an annual eleventh-grade trip to Jeju before the SAT-like suneung exam. The ferry left Incheon late on April 15, 2014, in heavy fog after the teachers considered canceling.

segments.title: Ship history and overloading
segments.summary: The Sewol was a former Japanese ferry that had served twenty years off Okinawa. The owner added passenger decks, expanded cargo space, and benefited from a Korean rule extending ferry life to thirty years. It carried over 2,100 tons of cargo, about a thousand tons over capacity.

segments.title: The sharp turn and listing
segments.summary: The third mate ordered a sudden turn around 8:45 am while the captain was off the bridge. Unsecured cargo shifted, and the ship listed about twenty degrees and did not right itself.

segments.title: In the Absence documentary
segments.summary: Hosts recommend the short New Yorker documentary In the Absence, which uses real-time communications to show the rescue failures as the ship sank.

segments.title: Passenger phone calls and first distress calls
segments.summary: Students had smartphones and messaged and called families while the ship listed. The first distress call to 119 came from a student about three minutes before the crew called for help. Crew asked the Coast Guard whether to evacuate and were told it was the captain's decision.

segments.title: Rescue delays and the captain's abandonment
segments.summary: Fishing boats rescued about half of survivors before the first Coast Guard boat arrived about 50 minutes after the turn. The captain left the ship without ordering evacuation. Passengers were told to stay in their cabins. Life rafts were insufficient and only one deployed automatically. Helicopter rescues were slow. Water flooded the ship and it sank within hours, with 304 trapped. Coast Guard ordered fishing boats to retreat.

segments.title: Break and news coverage
segments.summary: A brief break before returning. The hosts note the sinking was broadcast live on TV and that early misinformation said everyone was safe.

segments.title: Families' activism and government response
segments.summary: Families of the 250 students who died formed activist groups, held vigils, camped near the Blue House, and went on hunger strikes. The government and right-wing media attacked them, and officials surveilled and tapped their phones. Media was used to shift blame.

segments.title: Five buckets of blame
segments.summary: Hosts outline who failed: the captain and crew, cargo security, the ferry company, port inspectors, and the South Korean government. The Coast Guard was faulted, and it was reportedly dissolved as a result.

segments.title: Ferry company negligence and port inspection
segments.summary: The company cut corners and put profit ahead of safety. Inspectors checked freeboard by eye and did not inspect cargo. The company scuttled ballast to carry more cargo, making the ship unstable.

segments.title: Captain's trial and Yoo Byung-eun's death
segments.summary: Captain Lee Jun-seok was convicted of negligent homicide and sentenced to thirty-six years; he claimed he was stunned and gave conflicting testimony. The owner Yoo Byung-eun fled, was found dead in a plum orchard months later, and the government reportedly delayed announcing it.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break before the discussion of the government's response continues.

segments.title: President Park Geun-hye and her impeachment
segments.summary: President Park Geun-hye was absent for about seven hours and seemed poorly briefed. Related national security documents were sealed for thirty years. She was impeached in 2017 over a bribery case, and her sentence was later pardoned in 2022.

segments.title: Cause of the turn and unanswered questions
segments.summary: The sinking's cause remains unclear. The third mate testified she ordered a turn to avoid an oncoming ship, which radar seemed to support, but the quartermaster said he did not turn as hard as ordered.

segments.title: Other sentences and civil settlement
segments.summary: Ferry company CEO, shipping official, and private workers received prison terms. A 2018 civil court ordered compensation of about 600 million won per victim, roughly five hundred thirty thousand dollars. Eleven Coast Guard officers were tried, and the boat commander served four years.

segments.title: Surveillance convictions, memorial classroom, and Itaewon
segments.summary: Six Defense Security Command officers were convicted of illegally surveilling families. Parents formed activist groups and created the 4.16 Memorial classroom. The hosts mention the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush and families reaching out to victims' families.

segments.title: Families' demands and closing reflections
segments.summary: The families seek better government safety regulation and shipping requirements. The hosts reflect on the disaster and the captain's behavior and recommend the In the Absence documentary.

segments.title: Listener mail: homemade deodorant
segments.summary: A listener named Chris shares a recipe of coconut oil and baking soda, with optional essential oil. The hosts add a caution to dilute essential oils.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the listener mail address and sign off as a production of iHeartRadio.
